section.title: The Resurrection
section.sectionRationale: On the first day of the week the tomb is empty. An angel rolls back the stone and announces that Jesus has risen; the risen Lord meets the women and sends them to His brothers, while the guards are paid to spread a lie. Death is undone, and the news goes out.
section.thesis: Jesus has risen just as He said: the tomb is empty, the crucified Lord is alive and meets His own, calling them from fear to joy and worship, even as the authorities try to bury the truth under a bribe.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the empty tomb and the angel's announcement; the risen Jesus meeting the women; and the guards bribed to lie about the resurrection.

units.label: The empty tomb
units.note: He has risen, just as He said

verses.text: After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow.
The guards trembled in fear of him and became like dead men.
But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.
He is not here; He has {{egeiro|risen}}, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay.
Then go quickly and tell His disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead and is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.’ See, I have told you.”
So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great {{chara|joy}}, and ran to tell His disciples.

units.label: The risen Lord meets the women

verses.text: Suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” They came to Him, grasped His feet, and {{proskyneo|worshiped}} Him.
“Do not be afraid,” said Jesus. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me.”
While the women were on their way, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened.
And after the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money
and instructed them: “You are to say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep.’
If this report reaches the governor, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.”
So the guards took the money and did as they were instructed. And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day.

egeiro.gloss: To raise up, to wake, to raise from the dead. The angel's announcement, He has risen, is in the passive, He has been raised: God raised Jesus from the dead, vindicating His Son and defeating death, exactly as Jesus had foretold.

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness. The women leave the tomb with fear and great joy, the fitting response to the resurrection: awe at the holy power of God mingled with the overwhelming gladness that Jesus is alive.

proskyneo.gloss: To bow down, to worship. The women grasp the risen Jesus' feet and worship Him; the resurrection reveals Him as the proper object of worship, the risen Lord who is truly God with us.

basic.context: Early on Sunday, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb. An earthquake and an angel, bright as lightning, roll back the stone as the guards collapse in terror. The angel tells the women not to fear: Jesus is not here, He has risen as He said; they are to tell the disciples He will meet them in Galilee. Running with fear and great joy, they are met by the risen Jesus Himself, whom they worship. Meanwhile the guards report to the priests, who bribe them to spread the story that the disciples stole the body.
basic.hermeneutics: The resurrection is presented as a real event with witnesses, an empty tomb, and physical encounter. Note the two responses to the same empty tomb: the women worship, the leaders concoct a lie. That contrast, and the very existence of the theft story, are part of the evidence. Read the angel's just as He said: the resurrection vindicates all Jesus foretold.
basic.originalLanguages: The angel announces that Jesus has been egeiro, raised, by God. The women leave in fear and great chara, joy. And meeting the risen Lord, they proskyneo, worship Him.
basic.typology: Jesus rising on the third day fulfills the sign of Jonah and His own repeated predictions. The first day of the week, a new beginning, echoes the first day of creation, now the dawn of new creation.
basic.christ: Jesus is the risen Lord, alive after His crucifixion, vindicated by God, worthy of worship, and tenderly calling His failed disciples His brothers. Death could not hold Him; He is the conqueror of the grave.
basic.god: God raised Jesus from the dead, reversing the verdict of the cross and defeating death. He sends His angel to open the tomb and announce the news, and He turns even a hostile cover-up into unwitting testimony that the tomb was empty.
basic.crossReferences: Jonah 1 and Matthew 12 give the third-day sign. Psalm 16 promised God would not let His Holy One see decay. 1 Corinthians 15 declares the resurrection the foundation of the faith. Romans 1 says Jesus was declared Son of God by the resurrection.
basic.oneStory: The stone is rolled away, and the story turns from death to unending life. The crucified Jesus is risen, just as He said, and the same women who watched Him die now worship Him alive. Death, the last enemy since Eden, is broken. The cover-up cannot bury the empty tomb, and the risen Lord gathers His brothers for the mission that will carry this news to the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Matthew 28:1 to 15 is built as a diptych with a hinge. On one panel stand the women and the angel at the tomb, on the other the guards and the priests in the city, and the word 'Meanwhile' in verse 11 swings the camera from one to the other while the women are still on their way. The same event is told twice, once to people who worship and once to people who pay for silence.

The guard, who were the last characters of chapter 27, return here as the hinge. They are posted to keep the tomb shut and are 'shaken' by the earthquake in verse 4, and they become 'like dead men' while the one they guarded is alive. The reversal is the joke at the centre of the chapter: the dead man is the one who walks, and the living soldiers are the ones who fall. Matthew sets the empty tomb against the sealed tomb of 27:62 to 66 and shows which side wins.

There is a deliberate echo with the beginning of the Gospel. The angel's 'Do not be afraid' mirrors the angel's address to Joseph. Earthquakes frame Jesus' death in 27:51 and His rising in 28:2, and in each case heaven shakes the earth. Matthew also joins the two sections of the Gospel by the theme of Galilee: 'He is going ahead of you into Galilee' in verse 7 and verse 10 prepares the final scene on the mountain, 28:16 to 20.

The emotional line is carefully drawn. The women leave 'in fear and great joy,' two emotions in one breath, and the first word of the risen Jesus is a greeting and then 'Do not be afraid.' The movement from fear to worship and then to commission is the shape of the whole resurrection narrative, while the guards' path goes from fear to money to a lie.
context.historical:
The first day of the week is Sunday, the day after the Sabbath that had followed the Friday of the crucifixion. The women came, as Mark and Luke explain, with spices, but Matthew says only that they went 'to see the tomb,' possibly because he has already told us that the tomb was sealed and guarded. The tomb itself was a rock-cut chamber closed with a large rolling stone, and the angel's seat on the stone in verse 2 is a vivid detail: the stone meant to guard the entrance becomes a throne for God's messenger.

The women are the first witnesses, and that is itself a historical clue. In the ancient world a woman's testimony counted for little in many settings. Josephus says that Jewish courts did not admit it. If the early church had been inventing an account, it would hardly have chosen women as the first witnesses. All four Gospels do, and so Matthew's reader meets them without apology.

The guards are a Roman detachment, or possibly temple police, and their report to the chief priests rather than to Pilate suggests that they were under the priests' authority. The priests' offer of a 'large sum' recalls the thirty pieces paid to Judas and the money paid to the potter's field. The lie they invent is a strange one, because soldiers who were asleep could not know who took the body. The story that the disciples stole the body persisted: Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, reports that it was still being told by Jewish opponents of the church.

The promise that they would see Him in Galilee fits Jesus' own statement before His arrest, Matthew 26:32. Galilee was the region of His ministry and of most of the disciples, and Isaiah had called it 'Galilee of the nations,' Isaiah 9:1 and 2. Paul preserved a very early summary of the resurrection appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred and James, 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 8, which he says he received and passed on.
context.canonical:
The resurrection is the event that all the earlier Scriptures were waiting for, and Matthew's Gospel has marked it ahead of time. Jesus said that the Son of Man must be killed and raised on the third day, Matthew 16:21, and that the only sign given to that generation would be the sign of Jonah, three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:39 and 40. Hosea had spoken of being raised 'on the third day,' Hosea 6:2, and Psalm 16:10 had said that God would not abandon a faithful soul to Sheol or let His Holy One see decay, which Peter reads as David's prophecy of the Christ's resurrection, Acts 2:25 to 31.

The wider hope of the Old Testament also lies behind it. Isaiah foresaw that 'Your dead will live; their bodies will rise,' Isaiah 26:19, Daniel that many who sleep in the dust will awake, Daniel 12:2, and Ezekiel that the Lord would open graves and put His Spirit in His people, Ezekiel 37:12 to 14. Isaiah 25:8 promised that God would swallow up death forever. The angel's appearance, 'white as snow,' recalls the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9, and the face like lightning recalls the heavenly figure in Daniel 10:6.

The rest of the New Testament builds everything on this event. Paul says that the Son of God was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4, that Christ was 'delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification,' Romans 4:25, and that without the resurrection faith would be futile, 1 Corinthians 15:17. Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The followers soon meet on the first day of the week to break bread, Acts 20:7, and Revelation 1:10 knows it as the Lord's day.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote to give his readers certainty. The resurrection is told as a public event, with an angel, an earthquake, a stone moved, witnesses who saw and touched, and a rival explanation that confirms the tomb was empty. He did not write it as a pious legend. He closes the account by exposing the cover-up for what it was, so that no reader would be left thinking the question had never been asked.

He intended the resurrection to vindicate everything Jesus had said. The angel's 'just as He said' in verse 6 draws a line back through the whole Gospel to the predictions of Matthew 16:21, 17:23 and 20:19. What the disciples had not understood is now a fact. Jesus' word can be trusted because the thing He said would happen has happened.

He wanted to show the two possible responses to the same facts: worship from the women and a purchased lie from the priests. His readers must decide which road they will take. The Gospel offers no neutral position, and the empty tomb has to be explained either by the angel's word or by bribery.

Finally, he wanted the reader to see the tenderness of the risen Lord. Those who had fled are not rejected; they are called 'My brothers.' The word that opens the way to the Great Commission is forgiveness, and the Gospel is preparing the church to hear it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The text reports what happened at the tomb; it does not tell believers to look for angels or earthquakes. The women's actions, bowing and holding His feet, are a response to a unique event and not a liturgical rule, though worship of the risen Jesus is clearly right and Matthew presents it as such. The priests' bribe is recorded as sin, and no one is told to imitate the cover-up.

What carries forward is the message the angel gave and the Lord repeated: 'Do not be afraid' and 'go and tell.' The women are commissioned to speak before they understand it all, which is the pattern of the church's witness. The call to meet Jesus in Galilee reminds believers that the risen Lord is found in the ordinary places of ministry and obedience, not only in great moments.

The resurrection also grounds ethical hope. Paul says that because Christ has been raised, our labour is not in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58, and that we are to walk 'in newness of life,' Romans 6:4. The passage invites believers to live as people who know the end of the story.

One caution concerns the lie of verse 13. The text describes it as it was, and does not provide a template for responding to rumours, but it does show that a false story spreading widely and for a long time is not evidence for its truth: 'to this very day' is how long a lie can last.

debates.question: How is the empty tomb best explained?

views.label: God raised Jesus bodily
views.case: The tomb was empty because Jesus rose, as the Gospels and Paul's early creed say, 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 8. The many appearances to individuals and groups, including more than five hundred at once, and the sudden transformation of fearful disciples into witnesses, fit a real event better than any alternative.

views.label: The disciples stole the body
views.case: This is the earliest rival explanation, which Matthew himself reports in verse 13. It struggles because a Roman guard was posted, because disciples who had fled in fear would hardly have faced it, and because men do not usually die for what they know is a lie.

views.label: Visions, a mistaken tomb or a swoon
views.case: Other proposals suggest that grief produced visions, that the women went to the wrong grave, or that Jesus survived crucifixion. These do not account for the burial by Joseph at a known site, the Roman certainty of death, the bodily appearances where He ate and was touched, Luke 24:36 to 43, or the corporate nature of the sightings.

debates.bearing: The earliest preaching rested on the claim that the tomb was empty and that Jesus appeared, Acts 2:29 to 32. The question is not whether something happened, since every explanation grants that, but what. Matthew leaves the reader with the choice between the angel's word and the priests' bribe.

debates.question: What kind of body did Jesus have after the resurrection?

views.label: A real, physical body that has been transformed
views.case: In Matthew the women 'grasped His feet,' and in Luke He eats broiled fish and says a spirit does not have flesh and bones, Luke 24:39 to 43. The tomb is empty. Paul speaks of a 'spiritual body,' 1 Corinthians 15:44, which on this view means a body animated and transformed by the Spirit, not a body without matter.

views.label: A spiritual existence, not a physical one
views.case: Some argue that Paul's contrast between a natural and a spiritual body shows that the resurrection life is non-material. This reading has to explain away the empty tomb and the touching and eating in the Gospels.

views.label: A transformed physical body with new powers
views.case: The risen Jesus appears and vanishes, appears among them though the doors are locked, John 20:19, and is not at once recognised, yet He is flesh that can be touched. Many think this shows a body of the new creation, continuous with the old but not bound by its limits.

debates.bearing: Matthew's account fits the first and third views most naturally: the Jesus who meets the women is the same Jesus who died, and He can be held. The church's hope for its own bodies, Romans 8:11, depends on this continuity.

debates.question: Why does Jesus tell the women to go to Galilee, and how does this fit the other Gospels?

views.label: The Gospels record different appearances
views.case: Matthew emphasises Galilee, Luke and John emphasise Jerusalem, and both can be true. John 20 describes meetings in Jerusalem on the first evening and a week later, and Matthew 28:16 to 20 describes the gathering on a mountain in Galilee afterwards.

views.label: Matthew arranged the material by theme
views.case: Matthew concentrates on Galilee because it links back to the Gospel's opening, Matthew 4:12 to 16, and to the promise of Matthew 26:32, so that his final scene fulfils both.

views.label: The accounts conflict
views.case: Critics say the Gospels cannot be reconciled. Most readers reply that the Gospels are selective summaries and that their differences are what we would expect from independent witnesses.

debates.bearing: The angel and Jesus both say He is going ahead of them, which echoes the Shepherd imagery of Matthew 26:31 and 32. The instruction is a promise that the scattered flock will be gathered.

study.originalLanguages:
Matthew's Greek in verse 1 says literally 'after the Sabbaths, toward the first of the Sabbaths,' using the plural of 'Sabbath' for the week and a cardinal number, 'one,' where English would say 'first.' The BSB footnote preserves the oddity. It was an ordinary Jewish way to name the first day of a seven day cycle, and it marks the morning as a beginning: 'at dawn' is a verb that also means to begin to shine.

The earthquake in verse 2 and the guards' reaction in verse 4 are linked by a word play that English loses. The noun for earthquake and the verb for the guards being 'shaken' are from the same root, so that in effect the guards are 'earthquaked,' and they became 'like dead men.' The chapter's irony depends on that: the soldiers are shaken with the earth.

The angel says 'Do not be afraid,' and then, with emphasis, 'you,' in contrast to the guards: the Greek puts the pronoun forward, 'Fear not, you.' The word for 'looking for' in verse 5 is the common verb 'seek,' the one used of the hunt for the infant Jesus in Matthew 2:13, a quiet contrast between those who sought Him to kill Him and those who seek Him in love. 'He has risen' is a passive form, 'He has been raised,' and since Scripture speaks of God as the one who raises, the passive points to the Father's act, though the New Testament elsewhere says Jesus also rose by His own authority, John 10:18. The angel's 'just as He said' ties it back to the predictions of Matthew 16:21 and 17:23.

In verse 7 the angel says that Jesus 'is going ahead of you,' using the verb for a shepherd leading a flock, which Jesus used of Himself in Matthew 26:32 in the words 'I will go ahead of you into Galilee.' The word occurs there in the same context of the striking of the Shepherd and the scattering of the sheep. It is a small word with a large promise.

In verse 9 Jesus' greeting is the common Greek word that means both 'Hello' and 'Rejoice,' and it comes straight after 'great joy' in verse 8, so that the risen Lord's first word picks up the women's own emotion. The women 'grasped His feet,' a verb of firm holding that shows the bodily reality, and then they bowed in homage. The word 'brothers' in verse 10 is new: until now the disciples have been called 'disciples,' and after their desertion Jesus names them His family, as in Matthew 12:49 and 50. Hebrews 2:11 and 12 says He is not ashamed to call them brothers, quoting the psalm of the forsaken sufferer, Psalm 22:22.

The verb for the bribe, 'gave a large sum,' uses the word for 'sufficient,' with the sense of a worthy or ample price. And the closing phrase, 'to this very day,' echoes Matthew 27:8 about the Field of Blood, so that both a place and a lie are still in view when Matthew writes.

typology.fulfillment: Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, Jonah 1:17, and Jesus said that the Son of Man would spend three days in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40. Jonah came out alive to preach to a pagan city, which points to the nations hearing the good news. The correspondence is real because Jesus Himself draws it. The escalation is that Jonah was swallowed because of his own disobedience, while Christ goes into death out of obedience for others. The sign falls short in this: Jonah did not actually die, while Christ did.

typology.type: The first day of the week
typology.fulfillment: The first day of creation was the day God said 'Let there be light,' Genesis 1:3 to 5. Jesus rises on the first day of the week, and the early church came to meet on that day, Acts 20:7. Paul calls Christ 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the new creation begins with Him, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The link to the first day is an inference and not stated by Matthew, but it is a fitting one: the same God who began the old creation with light begins the new on the same day of the week. The type falls short because the old creation was good but fragile, while the new is secure.

typology.type: God's Holy One not abandoned to decay
typology.fulfillment: David wrote that God would not abandon his soul to Sheol or let His Holy One see decay, Psalm 16:10. Peter points out that David died and was buried and his tomb was still there, so he was speaking of the Christ, Acts 2:29 to 31. The tomb of David was occupied and the tomb of Jesus is empty. The pattern is that the righteous king trusts God beyond death, and Jesus fulfils it to the full, since His body saw no decay. David's hope was real for him too, but only in Christ is it accomplished.

The Shepherd of Zechariah 13:7 is struck and the sheep scattered. Jesus quotes it and promises to go ahead of them to Galilee, Matthew 26:31 and 32, and the angel and Jesus repeat the promise after the resurrection, verses 7 and 10. The risen Shepherd gathers the scattered flock. The picture continues in Hebrews 13:20, where God brings back from the dead 'the great Shepherd of the sheep.' The type is a pattern of the Shepherd's care, though Matthew does not use the word 'shepherd' in this scene.

study.christ:
The resurrection shows Jesus as the one who has conquered death and is now alive, with a body that can be held and a voice that can say 'Greetings.' The angel gives the news as a simple fact, 'He has risen,' and then points to the place: 'Come, see the place where He lay.' The faith the Gospel invites rests not on a theory but on an event with a location.

It is the vindication of the Crucified. The council condemned Him, the soldiers mocked Him, and Pilate's sentence stood. The resurrection is the Father's reversal of that verdict. Paul says Jesus was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4, and Peter told Jerusalem that 'God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ,' Acts 2:36. Everything He claimed, including the claim before Caiaphas that the Son of Man would sit at God's right hand, is now underwritten by the one who raised Him.

It is the sign of Jonah fulfilled and the third day of the Scriptures. He had told His disciples more than once that He would be raised, and here the promise is kept to the day. The resurrection also fulfils Psalm 16:10, and Peter makes the point that the body of David saw decay while the body of Jesus did not.

He is worthy of worship. The women bow and take hold of His feet, and He does not correct them. Later in the Gospel the disciples worship Him on the mountain, Matthew 28:17, and in the Bible worship is reserved for God alone, so Matthew presents the risen Jesus as the one to whom it is due. He is also the Lord of the new creation, 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18, and the one who says 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18.

He is the gracious Lord of failed disciples. The message He sends is to 'My brothers,' and the men who deserted Him at the arrest are the ones He names as family. The resurrection does not bring a reckoning with the deserters but a summons to meet Him. The Shepherd who was struck has come back for the scattered flock.

One caution keeps the reading honest. Matthew does not explain the resurrection by a metaphor, and we should not treat the angel, the earthquake or the stone as symbols that stand for something else. They are part of the event. The link to Christ is the event itself, understood as the New Testament understands it: the vindication of His claims and the first fruit of the new creation.
study.god:
The central statement about God here is that He raises the dead. The angel's 'He has risen' is in a form that points to the Father's action, and the apostles preach that 'God raised Him from the dead,' Acts 2:24. This is what the Old Testament's God does: He promised through Ezekiel to open graves and put His Spirit in His people, Ezekiel 37:12 to 14, and through Isaiah to swallow up death forever, Isaiah 25:8. The God of Israel is the God of life, and the empty tomb is His characteristic work.

He is faithful. The resurrection happens 'just as He said,' on the third day, and the details of the Old Testament are fulfilled with it. A God who keeps His word to the day can be trusted about what has not yet happened, including the resurrection of all who belong to Christ, Romans 8:11 and 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23.

He is sovereign over the powers that opposed Him. The leaders set a seal and a guard, which are the best Roman and priestly security, and a single messenger from heaven overturns them. The guards fall like dead men while the dead man lives. The rulers think they can manage the story with a bribe, and the story still spreads. Psalm 2 asks why the nations rage, and the answer in Matthew is that the one enthroned in heaven laughs at the plotting of kings.

He is just. The resurrection reverses the false verdict and also points to the day when He will judge the world by the man He appointed, and He 'has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead,' Acts 17:31. The resurrection is a ground of hope for believers and a warning to those who suppress the truth.

He is also gracious, and in a particular way. The first people He chooses to hear the news are women who were not admitted as witnesses in many courts, and the first word of the risen Son to the deserters is 'brothers.' The God of Matthew 28 chooses the weak, the overlooked and the failing as His messengers.

For worship, the resurrection calls for the response of the women, a mixture of fear and joy that turns into bowing, and then into going to tell. We worship a God who has not left His people in the grave and who will not leave them there.

crossReferences.note: Jesus said the Son of Man would spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, as Jonah did in the fish. The sign promised in Matthew 12 is the sign given in Matthew 28, and the repeated 'just as He said' connects the early prediction with the final fact.

David trusts that God will not abandon his soul to Sheol nor let His Holy One see decay. Peter argues in Acts 2 that David died and his tomb remained, so the psalm must point to the Christ. The empty tomb in Matthew 28 is the proof that the psalm was about Jesus.

Paul passes on what he received: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, over five hundred at once, and others. It is the earliest written summary, and it shows that Matthew's account stands within a wide public testimony.

Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The word 'firstfruits' means the beginning of the harvest, so the resurrection of Jesus promises that of His people. What happened in the garden tomb is the first part of what will happen to all who belong to Him.

The Shepherd is struck and the sheep are scattered, and Jesus quotes the verse before His arrest, Matthew 26:31. The promise 'I will go ahead of you into Galilee' in the next verse is kept in Matthew 28:7 and 10. The scattered flock is brought back by the Shepherd who was struck.

After two days He will revive us, and on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures,' and many hear this verse as one of them. It joins the nation's hope of restoration to the pattern of the Messiah.

John tells of Mary Magdalene weeping outside the tomb, mistaking Jesus for the gardener until He says her name, and being sent to tell 'My brothers.' It supplements Matthew's account, which is brief and shows the same pattern: the risen Lord meets a woman, and sends her to the others.

Jesus stands among the disciples and shows them His hands and feet, asks for something to eat and is given broiled fish. It supports Matthew's picture of a body that can be held. The risen Lord is not a ghost, which is just what the grasping of His feet implies.

Jesus was delivered over to death for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The resurrection is not only proof but part of the saving work, the declaration that the debt has been paid. What the women saw at the tomb is the basis for the believer's acceptance before God.

God has set a day to judge the world through the man He appointed and has given proof by raising Him from the dead. Paul uses the resurrection as the public sign that Jesus is the judge, so the empty tomb is a call to repent as well as a ground for joy.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a garden and a warning that disobedience would bring death, and the whole narrative afterward is the history of that death spreading, Genesis 2:17 and Romans 5:12. Matthew 28 is the point at which the sentence is overturned. A man has died, and a tomb in a garden, John 19:41, is empty on the first day of the week. The question every reader of Genesis 3 has to ask, whether the curse can be undone, receives its answer here.

The resurrection also completes the story of Israel. The nation had lived through exile, which the prophets called a death and a burial, and God had promised in Ezekiel 37 to open the graves and bring them up. Hosea spoke of being raised on the third day, and Isaiah of the dead living again. These were hopes for the nation, and in Jesus the Israel of one man goes through death and comes out the other side. The firstborn Son who was called out of Egypt, Hosea 11:1, is the one who now comes out of the grave.

It also launches what follows. The women are commissioned to tell, and the disciples are summoned to Galilee, where they will receive the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations. The Gospel that began with the genealogy of Abraham's son now reaches toward every nation, as God had promised Abraham, Genesis 12:3. The resurrection is the engine of mission, because the one who has all authority is the one who sends.

The cover-up in verses 11 to 15 shows that the story of resistance continues. The powers that conspired in the garden and in Jerusalem keep trying to bury what God has done. Yet the report 'has been circulated to this very day,' and so has the proclamation, and the second has outlasted the first.

The end is the new creation. Paul says that Christ is the firstfruits and that those who belong to Him will be raised at His coming, 1 Corinthians 15:23. John saw the risen Lord say, 'I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever,' Revelation 1:18. In the last chapters of the Bible a garden city appears, with the tree of life, and death is gone, 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The women who first heard 'He is not here' are the forerunners of a people who will hear 'He is here' and live with Him forever.

quiz.q: What did the angel announce at the empty tomb?

options.text: Jesus is not here; He has risen, just as He said, and will meet His disciples in Galilee.
options.note: Verses 6-7 give the angel's announcement of the resurrection foretold by Jesus.

options.text: That Jesus' body had been moved to another place.
options.note: The tomb was empty because He rose, not because the body was moved; this misses the resurrection.

options.text: That the disciples should mourn at the tomb.
options.note: The angel called them from fear to joyful proclamation, not mourning.

options.text: That Jesus would remain in the grave until the last day.
options.note: The angel declares He has already risen.

quiz.q: How did the women respond when the risen Jesus met them?

options.text: They grasped His feet and worshiped Him, with fear and great joy.
options.note: Verses 8-9 show worship of the risen Lord mixed with awe and joy.

options.text: They were glad to see a respected teacher again.
options.note: It was far more than seeing a teacher; they worshiped Him as Lord, which this understates.

options.text: They ran away in terror and told no one.
options.note: They were afraid but full of joy and ran to tell the disciples.

options.text: They did not recognize Him at all.
options.note: They recognized and worshiped Him at once.

quiz.q: How does the guards' bribe function in Matthew's account?

options.text: The cover-up concedes the tomb was empty and testifies, against the leaders' intent, to the resurrection.
options.note: The theft story assumes an empty tomb, undercutting itself as evidence.

options.text: It proves the disciples really did steal the body.
options.note: Matthew presents this as a paid-for lie, not the truth; the disciples had fled and despaired.

options.text: It shows the guards honestly reported what they saw.
options.note: They reported the truth first, then were bribed to spread a lie.

options.text: It has nothing to do with the resurrection.
options.note: It is directly about explaining away the empty tomb.

quiz.q: What is striking about Jesus calling the disciples His brothers after the resurrection?

options.text: He restores the very men who had fled and denied Him, meeting failure with grace.
options.note: Verse 10 shows the risen Lord's tender restoration of failing disciples.

options.text: He was simply being polite to His followers.
options.note: It is far more than politeness; it is gracious restoration after their desertion, which this misses.

options.text: He no longer regarded them as disciples.
options.note: Calling them brothers draws them closer, not further away.

options.text: He was rebuking them for abandoning Him.
options.note: His word is one of grace and restoration, not rebuke.

questions: The women came expecting a grave and found it empty. Where are you approaching a situation as final and closed that the risen Christ may yet transform?
They left the tomb with fear and great joy at once. How do awe at God's power and joy in the risen Christ live together in your own faith?
The risen Jesus called His deserting disciples His brothers. How does His grace toward those who failed Him encourage you when you have failed Him?
Faced with the same empty tomb, some worshiped and some lied. When the truth about Jesus confronts you, which response is more natural to you, and why?
The resurrection means death is defeated. How would truly believing that Jesus is alive change the way you face your fears this week?

translationNotes.note: The Greek is literally after the Sabbaths, at dawn toward the first of the Sabbaths; it marks the early morning of the first day of the week, Sunday, which became the Christian day of worship.
He has risen translates a passive form, He has been raised, pointing to the Father as the one who raised Jesus; just as He said ties the event to Jesus' own repeated predictions.
Matthew notes the stolen-body story was still circulating when he wrote; by recording it he answers the counter-claim, which itself presupposes an empty tomb.
